analysis.title: Midterm elections haven't radically changed economic growth
key_insights: US GDP composition (consumption, business investment, government spending) has stayed fairly consistent for decades, so elected officials have not re-engineered the economy.

Median annualized quarterly real GDP change has been similar under single-party Republican, single-party Democratic and divided government. The outlier divided-government quarters came from the COVID-19 shutdown and reopening.
Monetary policy often matters more for markets than the midterms. Politicians are helped or hurt by Fed efforts to ease or tighten financial conditions.
Since 1960 the president's party has lost 22 House seats on average in midterms. Only Clinton in 1998 and George W. Bush in 2002 gained seats.
President Trump's 41% average second-term approval rating suggests Republicans could potentially lose control of the House.
The S&P 500 has posted positive returns in the calendar year after midterms for nearly 65 years, regardless of the election outcome.
Markets have historically produced their weakest returns in a president's second year, the year leading into the midterms, and strong returns in year three, directly after the midterms.
Dow Jones average returns by presidential cycle year: Year 1 8.2%, Year 2 6.0%, Year 3 16.8%, Year 4 6.3%.

The report calls it a misconception that markets prefer divided government. Performance in the year after midterms has been strong under single-party rule and under different forms of divided government.

A hypothetical portfolio fully invested through Democratic and Republican administrations has outperformed one invested only when one party held power or during divided government. The report advises not letting election outcomes disrupt long-term plans.
risk_factors: Markets may be volatile in an election year.
Past performance does not guarantee future results.
